Big fan of history - I'm keenly aware of the fact that it is really, really, ridiculously difficult to get a Constitutional Amendment to go through (particularly in our era of do-nothing Congresses). However, I have to wonder - why hasn't there been a legitimate grassroots campaign to start up the process? There's plenty of ammunition to use out there of government abuse in this realm, I can't imagine it would be impossible to get people fired up about this.

It just seems to me that we are spending a lot of time being dictated to in terms of what the internet is and isn't, and I'm really tired of being treated like a default terrorist that needs his phone records combed.

So what's up with this, Voat? What would a good Digital Privacy Amendment include to maximize impact?
Why hasn't there been a push for a Constitutional Amendment for Digital Privacy beyond "it's really hard"?

Because what companies are doing online technically isn't any different than what they've been doing for years and years? They collect your data when you visit their space... They aren't getting into your private servers (except the NSA, etc and that is already supposed to be illegal), they are just aggregating data they have a reasonable right to collect on you anyway. See all of the stores that require you to give them a phone number, zipcode, etc before making a purchase.

The problem isn't that privacy doesn't exist but that lazy people want privacy in a public space. This is akin to someone in the mall food court yelling "Don't look at me!" If you want privacy it is something which must be actively pursued not assumed conducting your affairs in public.

In my mind, I see this more as a protection against excessively invasive practices by our own government. I totally agree that using certain products inherently loans itself to decreased privacy. But just because Facebook or Twitter can know and do certain things with private data doesn't mean that the NSA or other agencies should inherently have access to them.

And this problem is something that has been an issue for many years. There are already perfectly good laws in place preventing the collection of data by government agencies on it's citizens. The problem is that everybody tries to treat the internet specifically and networks and new technologies in general as completely new and unregulated areas. This isn't true. There are sufficient precedents to apply all existing laws concering how the government assembles and uses information on it's citizens (the application of search and seizure law to telephone tapping, etc). The law is written vaguely in reference to specific collection methods and specific properties intentionally, otherwise we would have to completely rewrite the law books every time a new model of phone came out, or every time the telephone company upgraded to a new switching system. The problem is that by demanding new laws to protect us, we the citizens denounce our protection under these existing laws. By calling for new laws to be enacted instead of existing laws being enforced we acknowledge that we aren't protected currently.

they've never amended the constitution to create an actual right to privacy. Instead, the populace waited long enough for an activist supreme court and now the right to privacy has become law. same thing will eventually happen with digital privacy and any other rights the majority of people feel is inherent in, implied by or understood as part of american liberties.

We have a Digital Privacy Amendment already. In fact, it's the fourth one they came up with, so it's been around for awhile. We don't need a new amendment that serves as nothing more than outlining specific use cases for another one. That's the function of the legislation, not the Constitution.

Searching The Volokh Conspiracy (A law blog- not a conspiracy theorist blog) has gotten a lot harder now that WaPo has mucked up the format, but try scanning through there for 4th amendment cases in the SCOTUS. The Obama administration has been taking a beating- often by unanimous decision. In an era of greater encroachment on the 4th amendment, a mixed ideology is mostly unanimous on this issue. You get the liberal "Oppressor vs. Oppressed" PoV generally weighing in against the government, and you get the more conservative Federalist approach that sits on the fact that the Constitution doesn't give you permission to do that.

Actually, as an aside, TVC pointed out that this is one of the most unified courts in history, even though all we hear about are the near-even splits.

That is fucking fantastic - thanks for sharing! And I agree with you on the Court - it's very weird how often they seem to be painted in a bad light. They've taken on some pretty high-stakes issues over the past few years (though I suppose that's essentially the point).

And in a politically charged time, it's easy to claim bias or prejudice or something like that.

But, again from TVC, if you really look into why justices do the things they do, I don't think that's the case. Occasional snide reference aside. As an example:

Justice Roberts voted twice against same-sex marriage and has been vilified for it. His reasoning, however, was a dissent against the manner in which the majority opinion chose to uphold SSM. By making it a 14th amendment issue, in Roberts' opinion, a very dangerous legal precedent has been set. But this is also the guy demanding to know how banning SSM is anything other than gender discrimination. He wanted to steer the issue down a different path.

But then, again from TVC, it's theorized that the 14th was used intentionally. Not as the most convenient way of passing an issue, but in order to set exactly the precedent that Roberts finds dangerous. Essentially (I'm not a lawyer- I'm a reader), this decision expands the 14th amendment from just applying to rights enumerated by the constitution to many more things the government does. Is this a good thing? Maybe. Is it dangerous? Probably. But that's for future courts to manage.

And then there's Scalia. Who, regardless of what he really thinks of SSM, is just of the opinion that the government has the right to only issue marriage licenses to couple of the opposite gender.

Reading through what I have on these SCOTUS cases, the more I think that bias has far, far less to do with anything than the pundits and the bloggers would have us believe. There are clearly vastly differing opinions on how to apply the Constitution. But I can't read everything I have about that and boil it down to "5 Enlightened vs. 4 Homophobes". And if these cases are more nuanced than we're led to believe, it seems to me that most, if not all of them, should be.
